newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA GENERATES PROFITS FROM REVIVING TOURISM.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA GENERATES PROFITS FROM REVIVING TOURISM.

text.p: Tourism to Bulgaria has boomed this year despite the country's economic crisis and the Tourism Committee expects revenue to total more than $900 million by year-end, officials said on Thursday.

"The basic economic results of the firms categorically confirm that even during a crisis in the country's development tourism can be a profitable sector," Tourism Committee President Vasil Velev told a news conference.
Velev said tourism revenue in 1995 totalled 14.6 billion levs, while for the first nine months of this year it was more than 22 billion levs.
However, tourist revenue is in foreign currency, whose value has appreciated sharply against a slumping lev.
Velev said net profit this year was expected to rise by more than 3.5 times against the net profit last year. The net profit for the first nine months of this year was more than 2.3 billion levs.
The number of foreign tourists, who were almost one million from January to October, is expected to rise by 15 percent for 1996 as a whole over last year.
"Our main goal for the last two years was to restore our position on traditional markets such as Russia and Central and East Europe," Velev said.
Bulgaria's Black Sea beaches and mountain ski resorts were a popular destination for East bloc tourists before the collapse of communism in 1989.

Germans were the most numerous foreign visitors this year so far, followed by tourists from Russia and the former Soviet republics mainly Ukraine and Belarus, the Scandinavian countries and Great Britain, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
Committee officials said they did not have the number of tourists from each country.
However, the Russians' return has compensated for a big drop in the number of western European visitors because of the country's bad image in its transition to a market economy.
The committee does not have enough funds to spend on promotion, Velev said.
Bulgaria's holiday resorts are state-owned but do not receive subsidies and rely on revenue to improve their facilities, Velev said.
More than 2.6 billion levs have been invested so far in renovating hotels and infrastructure against 1.7 billion for the whole of 1995, he added.
